title: Research Finds Risks of Eating Too Much Protein
paragraphs: High-protein foods have become extremely popular, with protein bars, shakes and snacks filling supermarket shelves. However, a new scientific review suggests that many people may be eating more protein than they need, and that too much protein may have some health risks.

The review was written by Bailey Knopf and Dudley Lamming of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and it was published in the journal Cell Press Blue in 2026. The researchers did not carry out a new experiment. Instead, they examined more than 350 earlier studies on protein and aging. According to Lamming, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need.

Much of the evidence came from studies on animals, such as flies, worms and rodents. In these studies, diets low in protein often improved metabolism and helped the animals live longer. The researchers explained that eating less protein reduces the activity of the body's main growth sensor, which is highly active when people eat a lot of protein. Low-protein diets also increase cells' ability to clean themselves, which may reduce inflammation. In addition, eating less protein raises the levels of a hormone called FGF21, which can improve blood sugar control. In one study, mice that were engineered to produce extra FGF21 lived about 30% to 40% longer.
In short-term studies on humans, people who reduced the amount of protein they ate lost weight and fat and had better blood sugar control.
The researchers also found that the type of protein may matter. Protein from plants has been linked to a lower risk of frailty in older age, while protein from animals has not.

However, there are important caveats. Nobody yet knows how eating less protein affects how long humans live. Exercise also makes a big difference. For example, athletes eat a lot of protein but rarely develop metabolic diseases. In addition, some groups need more protein, including pregnant women, growing children and people recovering from injuries. Many older adults already eat too little protein, so reducing it further could harm them.
Lamming suggested that protein recommendations should be based not only on a person's age, but also on how physically active they are.
